prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, which opened a new regime of precision in the measurement of time and frequency

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single prize part for B048, crediting Katori and Ye. The round-1 exchange has not weakened the scientific case; it has sharpened what the citation must say. The physics is a specific mechanism: a lattice at the magic wavelength makes the light shifts of the two clock levels equal, so that many neutral atoms can be held in the Lamb-Dicke regime, free of Doppler and recoil shifts, and be interrogated together. That combination gives narrow lines and a statistical signal-to-noise that a single trapped ion cannot match, and it is the reason these clocks sit at or below 1e-18 in systematic uncertainty. The evidence that matters to an experimentalist is replication, and here several independent laboratories and species have reached comparable levels and have compared clocks directly, including height differences at the millimetre scale. The chair asks for a credit split that can be defended. My reading is that Katori holds the magic-wavelength concept and an early realisation, while Ye's group holds the demonstrated record performance and the extension to many-body and spin-exchange effects inside the clock. Both parts are needed for the citation, and I do not see a cleaner pair anywhere on the shortlist. The impact is real beyond metrology: tests of the gravitational redshift, searches for drifting constants and ultralight dark matter, relativistic geodesy, and the preparation of a new definition of the second.
statement.case_against: The most serious objection, which every member raised, is that this might be read as an instrument advance one step downstream of the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize. I take that seriously and answer it on mechanism: neither earlier prize contains the magic-wavelength idea or the many-atom lattice interrogation, so the citation must name the lattice clock and nothing broader. The second objection is credit. Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Boyd, Hollberg and the Yb, Hg and ion-clock groups all contributed, and with a limit of three names I cannot claim two names capture the whole community; I only claim they capture the decisive concept and the decisive demonstrated performance. Third, several of us, myself included, are stating the chronology from memory (Katori's proposal around 2003, the first strontium lattice clocks around 2005 to 2006, Ye's accuracy records later). I cannot verify exact dates or record values from primary papers inside this exercise, and I do not want the convergence in round 1 to be treated as if it had been checked.

responses.point: Eriksson concedes that his own B019 has a weak attribution (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu and Moore missing, and the 2016 topology prize nearby) but still raises the purist objection that the lattice clock is an instrument advance and not a new physical discovery.
responses.response: I accept that the B019 credit problem is a real defect, and I appreciate that he says a weak attribution is a worse flaw than a modest novelty question; I agree with that ordering. On the purist objection, I would point to the many-body physics that he and Johansson cite: a degenerate lattice of neutral atoms with spin-exchange interactions is a controllable quantum many-body system that is also the best clock, and the interaction shifts had to be understood in order to reach 1e-18. A prize for a method that creates a new regime of physics and a new measuring capability fits the committee's history for precision spectroscopy. I would still word the citation narrowly so it does not read as a general prize for clocks.

responses.point: Mehlig says he would be more concerned if either Katori or Ye were dropped than about the split between them, and that the citation must show distinctness from the 2005 and 2012 prizes; he has also withdrawn his own B011 for this year.
responses.response: I agree that dropping either name would be the larger error, and I would not try to rank them in the citation. On wording, I think the distinctness is best shown by naming the mechanism-bearing object (the optical lattice clock) and avoiding phrases such as time and frequency measurement in general, which would invite the objection that 2005 already covered it. I would accept either of the two citation variants that circulated in round 1 on that condition; mine mentions a new regime of precision, which also keeps the second and the many-body results open. I respect his decision to set aside B011 and do not think the committee loses a defensible alternative by it.

responses.point: Olsson asks for a check of Katori's priority against the 2003 to 2005 papers, concludes the clock is a distinct invention because it needs the magic-wavelength idea, and still thinks she may undervalue the Higgs case, held back only by the three-name problem.
responses.response: As far as I recall, the chronology supports her reading: Katori and co-workers proposed the engineered light-shift (magic-wavelength) trap around 2003, and the first lattice clock spectroscopy in strontium followed from his group and soon after from Ye's group and from SYRTE. I cannot confirm exact dates from primary papers here, so I would state it as my recollection and not as verified. It does favour Katori on priority and Ye on record performance, and does not change the two-name set. On Higgs, I still see no principled rule that picks three of four names from ATLAS and CMS, and she has not offered one; if a rule appeared I would reconsider, but I do not think it is on the table for this year.

responses.point: Danielsson has moved from his opening choice (EHT) to B048 on grounds of defensibility, says he cannot adjudicate the Katori and Ye relationship from the text, and asks whether the pending SI redefinition should make recognition wait.
responses.response: I do not think he has to adjudicate a relationship: a prize does not need to settle who did what first beyond the decisive contributions, and the two groups' contributions are different in kind (concept and first realisation, versus record accuracy and many-body control). On timing, my view is the same as in round 1. The redefinition is a consequence of these clocks and not a test of whether they work, because the 1e-18 uncertainties have been reproduced already. Waiting also adds risk, since the lattice-clock community keeps growing and the attribution will become harder, not easier, to defend with three names. I would not treat B052 as a reason to hesitate: his own EHT credit has the imaging-algorithm and station-leader problem that he names.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair and an astroparticle specialist, relies on the atomic-physics members for the lattice-clock chronology and raises whether a two-part prize combining the clock with another part is needed.
responses.response: He is right to ask the atomic-physics members for the chronology, and I have tried to answer above while saying what I cannot verify. On a second part, I considered it honestly. B025 is attractive on sensitivity, but combined with B048 it would need five names against a limit of three in total, and the priority among Borde, Pritchard and Kasevich, with Chu already recognised in 1997, is less settled than Katori and Ye. I would not force a second part for the sake of breadth. A single sharp prize is easier to defend than a combination that depends on contested credit.

responses.point: Johansson says the redefinition should not be used either as a reason to wait or to act, and flags B001 as a possible recusal matter for him.
responses.response: I largely agree on the redefinition: I would not make it the reason for the prize, only note that it removes the argument that the clock has no practical use. On B001, his disclosure is the right one and, together with the 2025 prize, it keeps circuit QED out of my configuration. My own WACQT link with Chalmers is institutional and does not touch B048. If B001 came back I would support recording his recusal and I would not count his preference as part of any support.

uncertainties: Whether the full committee accepts the clock as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes; I judge it on the mechanism but it remains a judgement.

The exact priority chronology (Katori 2003 proposal, first strontium lattice clocks around 2005 to 2006, Ye's later accuracy records) and the 1e-18 record values are from memory and not checked against primary papers.
Whether Lemonde, Takamoto or others have a claim strong enough to join or displace one of the two names; I have not seen a documented ground for it.
Whether to include the second and the redefinition in the citation; I prefer wording about the optical lattice clock and a new regime of precision.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with Katori or Ye in the B048 configuration. For full disclosure, during my PhD I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Ye is associated with that JILA environment; I have no joint work, financial tie or documented overlap in time with Ye, and I do not consider this a recusal matter. My WACQT role overlaps institutionally with Chalmers (Johansson's home), which matters for B001 and not for this configuration. I have no new disclosure after round 1.
